 In brief 
 Workflow automation maps your business processes, identifies high-ROI candidates for automation, and builds them. Done well, it recovers 20-40% of admin time. We score every candidate against time saved, error reduction, and payback period — and only build the ones that justify the fee. 
 
 What workflow automation looks like in practice 
 Common workflows we automate for mid-market UK clients: 
 
 Lead-to-customer — capturing leads, scoring, routing, sequenced follow-up, handover to sales. 
 Quote-to-cash — quote generation, e-signature, invoicing, payment reminders. 
 Onboarding — new client/employee onboarding with task assignment, document collection, and welcome flows. 
 Approval flows — invoice approval, expense approval, holiday requests with multi-stage routing. 
 Reporting — automated weekly dashboards pulling from CRM/finance/ops. 
 

 How we score automation ROI 
 
 Time mapping — how many hours/month does this workflow consume? 
 Loaded cost — at the loaded cost of the people running it, what's the £-value? 
 Build cost — what does it cost to automate (build + tooling + ongoing)? 
 Payback period — when does the £-saved cross the £-spent line? 
 
 We only build automations with a payback period under 12 months, ideally under 6. 

 Tools we use 
 Tool-agnostic — we choose based on your stack, your team's skills, and what's maintainable. 
 
 Low-code: Zapier, Make, n8n, Power Automate 
 iPaaS: Workato, Tray.io for higher-complexity 
 Custom: Node, Python, serverless functions for non-standard integrations 
 RPA: UiPath where there's no API option

Sydney-based, working across Australia. Book a Discovery Call → Take the free assessment What does a business automation agency do? A business automation agency finds the repeating work inside a company, decides which of it can safely be handled by software, and then builds and deploys that software. The work splits three ways: mapping the processes and costing them in hours, building the automation and connecting it to the systems the business already runs on, and putting governance around anything that runs unattended. The distinction that matters when choosing one is delivery — an agency that stops at a recommendation has done the first third and left you to buy the rest. The honest comparison Agency, independent consultant, or hire in-house? All three work. They fail in different ways, and the right answer depends on how much automation you expect to do after the first one. Three ways to get business automation built, and what each one costs you Automation agency Independent consultant In-house hire Typical cost Fixed fee per build, from $3,500 AUD $120–$250/hr, open-ended $120K–$180K/yr fully loaded Time to first result One to eight weeks Depends on their availability Three months before they know your systems Who owns it after You do, with a written playbook Usually you, sometimes them They do — until they leave Breadth of skills Whole team: process, build, integration, governance Whatever that one person is good at Whatever that one person is good at How it fails Scope creep, or a retainer you cannot leave They get busy with another client Key-person risk, and it takes a year to notice Best when You want two or three automations live this quarter You have one narrow, well-understood problem Automation is a permanent, continuous function Our fixed fees are published rather than quoted on request: $3,500 AUD for a Claude Cowork setup, around $8,000 for a multi-team implementation, and from around $10,000 for a Claude Code rollout. How we actually run an automation engagement Hours first, tools second Find the repeating work We map the processes that repeat and cost them in hours and AUD before proposing anything. Most businesses are surprised by which process is actually the expensive one — it is rarely the one that feels most annoying. The step most proposals skip Check the data can be reached Software can only act on what it can get to. Files in someone’s inbox, figures that live in a spreadsheet on one laptop, and approvals that happen verbally are all blockers that no tool solves. We find these before quoting, not after. Working, not demonstrated Build one thing and put it in production One workflow, end to end, running against real data with real failure handling. A pilot that works on curated inputs proves nothing about the Tuesday when the file arrives malformed. Governance in writing Write down what runs unattended Which steps run on their own, which always ask first, what happens when something fails silently, and who is allowed to change that list. This is the part that decides whether an automation is still running in six months. You own it Hand it over The workflows, the configuration and a written playbook your team can extend. We do not build dependencies on ourselves — a retainer you cannot leave is a business model, not an outcome.
